html:
In 1025 and 1026 Mahmud of Ghazni led an army across the desert to the temple of Somnath on the coast of Gujarat, one of the holiest shrines of Shiva in India. He broke its idol and carried off a vast treasure.

Mahmud ruled the Ghaznavid state from Ghazni in Afghanistan from 998 to 1030. He raided northern India about seventeen times, mostly for loot to pay his army and adorn his capital, and also as holy war. Somnath was the farthest and most famous of these raids. He annexed the Punjab, but did not try to rule the rest.

The raid left a long memory. Persian chroniclers praised it as a triumph of Islam; later Hindu and nationalist writers made it a symbol of conquest and loss. The temple was rebuilt many times, most recently after Indian independence in 1951. Mahmud's companion al-Biruni wrote a careful account of India in the same years.
